options.text: It is composed of smooth muscle cells and collagen
options.explanation: The fibrous cap overlying the lipid core is composed of smooth muscle cells, collagen, and extracellular matrix.

options.text: It is primarily composed of foam cells
options.explanation: Foam cells are in the lipid core.

options.text: It is resistant to rupture when thin
options.explanation: Thin caps are more vulnerable to rupture.
It contains vasa vasorum.
Fibrin is part of thrombus, not the fibrous cap.

explanation.overview: The fibrous cap is a dynamic structure synthesized by vascular smooth muscle cells. A thick cap with more collagen and SMCs is stable; a thin cap with inflammation and few SMCs is vulnerable.
explanation.highYield: Fibrous cap: SMCs, collagen. T‑lymphocytes and macrophages produce MMPs that degrade cap → rupture.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Statins stabilize plaques by reducing inflammation and promoting collagen deposition.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of aortic regurgitation in developing countries?

options.explanation: Rheumatic valve disease remains a leading cause of aortic regurgitation in developing nations.
Bicuspid valve is a common cause in developed countries.
Aortic root dilation is common in developed countries.
Endocarditis is less common.
Syphilis is now rare.

explanation.overview: Globally, rheumatic heart disease is the most common cause of aortic regurgitation, particularly in low‑ and middle‑income countries. In developed countries, degenerative and congenital causes predominate.
explanation.highYield: Aortic regurgitation etiology: rheumatic (developing), bicuspid valve and aortic root disease (developed).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Rheumatic prophylaxis with penicillin prevents recurrence.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common cardiac manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus?

options.explanation: Pericarditis is the most common cardiac manifestation of SLE, occurring in up to 40% of patients.
Myocarditis is less common.
Libman‑Sacks endocarditis is classic but less frequent.
Coronary involvement is rare.
Valvular stenosis is uncommon.

explanation.overview: SLE can affect the heart in multiple ways: pericarditis (most common), myocarditis, Libman‑Sacks endocarditis, and accelerated atherosclerosis. Pericarditis may be symptomatic or asymptomatic.
explanation.highYield: SLE heart: pericarditis > myocarditis > Libman‑Sacks endocarditis. Also increased CAD risk.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Pericarditis in SLE is treated with NSAIDs or corticosteroids.

questions.question: Which of the following best differentiates constrictive pericarditis from restrictive cardiomyopathy?

options.text: Respiratory variation in mitral inflow velocities and septal bounce on echocardiography
options.explanation: Constrictive pericarditis shows marked respiratory variation in mitral inflow and tissue Doppler velocities, and a septal bounce (ventricular interdependence).
Both can have elevated JVP.
Both can cause edema.
Hepatomegaly occurs in both.
Both have diastolic dysfunction.

explanation.overview: Distinguishing constrictive pericarditis from restrictive cardiomyopathy is critical. Echocardiography, cardiac catheterization (dip‑plateau sign), and MRI/CT help. Enhanced ventricular interdependence with respiration favors constriction.
explanation.highYield: Constriction: respiratory variation, septal bounce, preserved tissue Doppler velocities. Restriction: blunted tissue Doppler, no significant respiratory variation.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Constrictive pericarditis is potentially curable with pericardiectomy.

questions.question: Which of the following is a recognized cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy?

options.explanation: Endomyocardial fibrosis is a cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy, endemic in tropical regions.
Hypertension causes LVH, not restrictive CM.
Ischemia causes DCM or ischemic CM.
Doxorubicin causes DCM.
Alcohol causes DCM.

explanation.overview: Restrictive cardiomyopathy has multiple causes including infiltrative (amyloidosis, sarcoidosis), storage (hemochromatosis, Fabry disease), and endomyocardial (endomyocardial fibrosis, Löffler).
explanation.highYield: Restrictive CM causes: amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, radiation, endomyocardial fibrosis, hypereosinophilic syndrome.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Endomyocardial fibrosis involves fibrosis of the inflow tract and apex, causing obliteration and restrictive physiology.

questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of acute rheumatic fever?

options.explanation: Aschoff bodies are pathognomonic granulomatous lesions with Anitschkow cells and central fibrinoid necrosis, found in acute rheumatic carditis.
Commissural fusion occurs in chronic rheumatic disease.
Calcification is a late sequela.
Rheumatic vegetations are small and sterile.
Perforation is typical of infective endocarditis.

explanation.overview: Acute rheumatic fever is a post‑streptococcal inflammatory disease affecting heart, joints, skin, and brain. Pancarditis with Aschoff bodies is characteristic.
explanation.highYield: Acute RF: Aschoff bodies (Anitschkow caterpillar cells), pancarditis. Diagnosed by Jones criteria. Can progress to chronic RHD.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Prevention with penicillin for strep throat prevents acute rheumatic fever.

questions.question: A 40‑year‑old woman with known mitral valve prolapse presents with fever and a new murmur. Blood cultures grow Streptococcus viridans. Which valve is most likely affected?

options.explanation: Mitral valve prolapse is a predisposing factor for infective endocarditis, most commonly affecting the mitral valve.
Aortic valve is also possible but mitral is more common in MVP.
Tricuspid is more common in IV drug users.
Pulmonic is rarely involved.
She has native MVP, not prosthetic.

explanation.overview: Mitral valve prolapse with regurgitation creates a nidus for bacterial adherence, leading to subacute bacterial endocarditis. Prophylactic antibiotics are no longer routinely recommended except for high‑risk patients.
explanation.highYield: MVP → increased risk of endocarditis, especially with regurgitation. Most common organism: Streptococcus viridans.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Infective endocarditis in MVP can cause chordal rupture and worsening regurgitation.

questions.question: Which of the following is the primary defect in arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC)?

options.text: Fibrofatty replacement of right ventricular myocardium
options.explanation: ARVC is characterized by progressive replacement of RV myocardium by fibrofatty tissue, leading to arrhythmias and sudden death.
Myocyte disarray is characteristic of HCM.
Amyloidosis is a restrictive CM.
Iron overload causes DCM.
Granulomas are typical of sarcoidosis.

explanation.overview: ARVC is a genetic cardiomyopathy with autosomal dominant inheritance, often involving desmosomal gene mutations (plakoglobin, desmoplakin). It presents with ventricular arrhythmias and risk of sudden death.
explanation.highYield: ARVC: fibrofatty replacement of RV, epsilon wave on ECG, RV dysfunction. Common cause of sudden death in young athletes.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Diagnosis by modified Task Force criteria (imaging, ECG, family history). ICD for high‑risk patients.

questions.question: A 30‑year‑old man collapses during a basketball game. Autopsy shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy and myocyte disarray. He most likely had:

options.explanation: Young athlete with asymmetric septal hypertrophy and myocyte disarray is classic for HCM.
DCM shows dilation, not asymmetric hypertrophy.
ARVC involves fibrofatty replacement of RV.
Myocarditis shows inflammation.
Coronary anomaly can cause sudden death but histology would show ischemic changes, not disarray.

explanation.overview: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the most common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes. It is characterized by asymmetric septal hypertrophy, myocyte disarray, and fibrosis.
explanation.highYield: HCM = sudden death in young athletes. Screening: echocardiography. Prophylactic ICD in high‑risk patients.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: First‑degree relatives should be screened.

questions.question: Which of the following is a cause of secondary hypertension?

options.explanation: Renal artery stenosis leads to activation of RAAS, causing hypertension.
Essential hypertension has no identifiable secondary cause.
White coat hypertension is not secondary.
Labile hypertension may be idiopathic.
Isolated systolic hypertension is usually age‑related.

explanation.overview: Secondary hypertension has an identifiable cause: renal (renal artery stenosis, glomerulonephritis), endocrine (Cushing, pheochromocytoma, primary aldosteronism), vascular (coarctation), or drugs (NSAIDs, OCPs).
explanation.highYield: Renal artery stenosis → renovascular hypertension (increased renin). In young women, consider fibromuscular dysplasia.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Renal artery angioplasty can cure hypertension in select cases.

questions.question: A 20‑year‑old woman presents with hypertension and a systolic murmur heard over the back. Chest X‑ray shows rib notching. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Coarctation of the aorta causes hypertension in the upper extremities, hypotension in lower extremities, and collateral circulation causing rib notching (Roesler sign).
Aortic stenosis does not cause rib notching.
PDA causes continuous murmur, not rib notching.
ASD has no rib notching.
VSD does not cause rib notching.

explanation.overview: Coarctation of the aorta is a congenital narrowing, typically distal to the left subclavian artery. It leads to upper extremity hypertension, weak femoral pulses, and collateral vessels eroding ribs (notching).
explanation.highYield: Coarctation: hypertension (upper extremities), weak femoral pulses, rib notching (3rd–8th ribs). Associated with bicuspid aortic valve and Turner syndrome.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Surgical or catheter‑based repair restores normal hemodynamics.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about the ductus arteriosus?

options.text: It normally closes within the first few days after birth
options.explanation: Functional closure occurs within 24–48 hours, with anatomic closure over weeks.

options.text: It connects the aorta and left pulmonary artery
options.explanation: It connects the aorta (descending) to the left pulmonary artery.

options.text: It remains open in most adults
options.explanation: Normally closes; patent ductus arteriosus is abnormal.

options.text: It shunts blood from left to right in fetal life
options.explanation: In fetal life, it shunts from right to left (bypassing lungs).

options.text: It carries oxygenated blood in the fetus
options.explanation: It carries deoxygenated blood from pulmonary artery to aorta.

explanation.overview: The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary artery to the descending aorta, allowing fetal blood to bypass the lungs. It normally closes soon after birth; failure to close results in patent ductus arteriosus (PDA).
explanation.highYield: PDA: continuous machinery murmur. Left‑to‑right shunt. Treat with indomethacin or surgical closure.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: PDA is common in premature infants; it can cause heart failure if large.

questions.question: Which of the following is a cyanotic congenital heart disease?

options.explanation: Tetralogy of Fallot is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease beyond infancy.
ASD is acyanotic.
VSD is usually acyanotic.
PDA is acyanotic.
Coarctation is acyanotic.

explanation.overview: Cyanotic congenital heart diseases include Tetralogy of Fallot, transposition of the great arteries, truncus arteriosus, tricuspid atresia, and total anomalous pulmonary venous return.
explanation.highYield: Tetralogy of Fallot: VSD, overriding aorta, RV outflow obstruction, RV hypertrophy. 'Boot‑shaped' heart. Squatting spells.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Surgical correction is usually done in infancy.

questions.question: Which of the following is a paraneoplastic syndrome associated with cardiac myxoma?

options.text: Fever, weight loss, arthralgias, and elevated IL‑6
options.explanation: Cardiac myxomas can produce IL‑6, causing constitutional symptoms and mimicking autoimmune disease.
Cushing syndrome is associated with ectopic ACTH, not myxoma.
SIADH is associated with small cell lung cancer.
Hypercalcemia is associated with squamous cell carcinoma.
Polycythemia may occur with cerebellar hemangioblastoma.

explanation.overview: Myxomas can secrete interleukin‑6, causing systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, malaise, arthralgias) and laboratory abnormalities (anemia, elevated ESR/CRP). These resolve after tumor removal.
explanation.highYield: Myxoma paraneoplastic: IL‑6 production → constitutional symptoms, anemia. Can mimic infective endocarditis or vasculitis.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Surgical excision is curative and reverses the paraneoplastic syndrome.

questions.question: Which of the following is a known risk factor for infective endocarditis?

options.explanation: IV drug use is a major risk factor for right‑sided endocarditis, often due to S. aureus.
Hypertension is not a direct risk factor.
Obesity is not a direct risk factor.
Diabetes is not a strong risk factor unless associated with other conditions.
Hypothyroidism is not a risk factor.

explanation.overview: Risk factors for infective endocarditis include structural heart disease (valvular disease, congenital heart disease), prosthetic valves, previous IE, IV drug use, and invasive procedures causing bacteremia.
explanation.highYield: IE risk factors: prosthetic valves, previous IE, unrepaired cyanotic CHD, IV drug use, poor dentition. Prophylaxis guidelines focus on highest‑risk patients.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Good dental hygiene and avoiding unnecessary IV lines reduce risk.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of acute rheumatic carditis?

options.explanation: Acute rheumatic fever involves all layers of the heart (pancarditis), with pathognomonic Aschoff bodies in the myocardium.
It is pancarditis, not isolated pericarditis.
Rheumatic endocarditis has small, warty vegetations.
Giant cells are not a feature.
Valvulitis is part of pancarditis.

explanation.overview: Acute rheumatic carditis is a pancarditis (endocarditis, myocarditis, pericarditis). Aschoff bodies are granulomatous lesions with central fibrinoid necrosis, Anitschkow cells, and Aschoff giant cells.
explanation.highYield: Rheumatic carditis: pancarditis, Aschoff bodies, mitral valve most involved. Jones criteria for diagnosis.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Valvular sequelae (mitral stenosis) develop years later.

questions.question: Which type of necrosis is characteristic of myocardial infarction?

options.explanation: MI results in coagulative necrosis, with preservation of cell outlines and eventual removal by macrophages.
Liquefactive necrosis occurs in brain infarcts.
Caseous necrosis is typical of tuberculosis.
Fat necrosis is seen in pancreatitis.
Fibrinoid necrosis is typical of vasculitis.

explanation.overview: Ischemic death of cardiac myocytes results in coagulative necrosis, where cellular architecture is preserved but nuclei are lost. It is followed by inflammation and eventually fibrosis.
explanation.highYield: MI = coagulative necrosis. Reperfusion can cause contraction band necrosis. Final outcome: collagenous scar.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Time course of histologic changes helps date the infarct.

questions.question: Which of the following is a cause of non‑atherosclerotic coronary artery disease?

options.explanation: Vasculitis, including Kawasaki disease and PAN, can cause coronary artery abnormalities.
Smoking promotes atherosclerosis.
Dyslipidemia causes atherosclerosis.
Age is a risk factor for atherosclerosis.
Male sex is a risk factor for atherosclerosis.

explanation.overview: Non‑atherosclerotic causes of coronary artery disease include vasculitis (Kawasaki, PAN, Takayasu), dissection (spontaneous coronary artery dissection – SCAD), embolism, spasm, and congenital anomalies.
explanation.highYield: SCAD: young women, pregnancy‑associated. Coronary vasculitis: Kawasaki, PAN. Embolism: endocarditis, AF.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Management differs from typical atherosclerotic CAD.

questions.question: A 25‑year‑old woman presents with an acute MI. Coronary angiography shows a dissection. Which condition is most likely?

options.explanation: SCAD is a non‑atherosclerotic dissection occurring predominantly in young women, often associated with pregnancy, fibromuscular dysplasia, or connective tissue disorders.
Young woman without risk factors makes atherosclerosis unlikely.
Embolism would show a filling defect, not dissection.
Vasculitis could cause aneurysms but dissection is classic for SCAD.
Bridge shows systolic compression.

explanation.overview: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is an important cause of MI in young women without traditional risk factors. It is often associated with pregnancy, fibromuscular dysplasia, and extreme stress.
explanation.highYield: SCAD: young women, pregnancy, FMD. Tear in coronary media → hematoma → lumen compression. Conservative management often preferred.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: PCI or CABG reserved for high‑risk cases.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a classic feature of infective endocarditis?

options.explanation: Janeway lesions are painless hemorrhagic macules, a classic peripheral sign.
Osler nodes are painful nodules on fingers/toes, a classic sign.
Roth spots are retinal hemorrhages with pale centers.
Splinter hemorrhages are linear nail bed hemorrhages.
Kerley B lines are a chest X‑ray finding in pulmonary edema, not specific to endocarditis.

explanation.overview: Classic peripheral signs of infective endocarditis include Janeway lesions (painless), Osler nodes (painful), splinter hemorrhages, Roth spots, and glomerulonephritis. Kerley B lines indicate pulmonary edema.
explanation.highYield: IE stigmata: Osler nodes (painful, immune), Janeway lesions (painless, septic emboli), Roth spots, splinter hemorrhages.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: These signs are more common in subacute IE.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about the treatment of acute rheumatic fever?

options.text: Antibiotics are given to eradicate streptococcal carriage and prevent recurrence
options.explanation: Acute rheumatic fever requires initial treatment of group A strep (penicillin) and long‑term antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent recurrence.
Antibiotics do not reverse existing damage.
Corticosteroids are used for severe carditis but not always.

options.text: Surgical valve replacement is first‑line for acute carditis
options.explanation: Surgery is for chronic valve disease, not acute episode.
NSAIDs are used for arthritis.

explanation.overview: Primary prevention of rheumatic fever involves treating strep pharyngitis. In established RF, antibiotics eradicate organisms and ongoing prophylaxis prevents recurrences, which can worsen valvular damage.
explanation.highYield: Penicillin prophylaxis (monthly benzathine penicillin) for at least 5 years, often longer. Prevents recurrent RF and progression of RHD.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Secondary prevention is crucial in endemic areas.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common congenital heart disease in adults?

options.explanation: Bicuspid aortic valve is the most common congenital cardiovascular anomaly, present in about 1‑2% of the population.
ASD is common but less than BAV.
VSD is the most common congenital heart disease at birth but many close spontaneously.
PDA is less common.
Coarctation is less common.

explanation.overview: Bicuspid aortic valve is the most common congenital heart defect, often undiagnosed until adulthood when it presents with stenosis, regurgitation, or endocarditis.
explanation.highYield: BAV: most common congenital heart disease. Associated with aortopathy (root dilation, coarctation). Screening of first‑degree relatives.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Echocardiography is used for surveillance.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of cardiac tamponade on echocardiography?

options.text: Right atrial and right ventricular diastolic collapse
options.explanation: Echocardiographic findings in tamponade include RA systolic collapse and RV diastolic collapse, reflecting compression when pericardial pressure exceeds chamber pressure.
LVH is a sign of chronic pressure overload.
AR is valvular disease.
VSD is a congenital shunt.
LA dilation occurs in mitral valve disease.

explanation.overview: Echocardiography is the diagnostic modality of choice for tamponade. Key features include pericardial effusion with RA/RV collapse, respiratory variation in mitral and tricuspid inflow velocities, and a dilated IVC with blunted respiratory collapse.
explanation.highYield: Tamponade echo: RA systolic collapse, RV diastolic collapse, IVC plethora, respiratory variation. Emergent pericardiocentesis.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Clinical assessment (Beck triad, pulsus paradoxus) combined with echo confirms diagnosis.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about the natural history of an abdominal aortic aneurysm?

options.text: The risk of rupture increases with aneurysm size
options.explanation: AAA rupture risk increases exponentially once the diameter exceeds 5.5 cm.
Small aneurysms have a lower risk but can still rupture.
Many patients die of other causes before rupture.
Most ruptures occur without warning symptoms.
Calcification does not protect.

explanation.overview: AAA growth rate is variable. The risk of rupture rises sharply with diameter >5.5 cm. Elective repair is recommended at this threshold to prevent rupture, which carries >80% mortality.
explanation.highYield: AAA: rupture risk ~1%/year for 5.0‑5.4 cm, >10%/year for ≥6 cm. Screening ultrasound for 65‑75 year old male smokers.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Open surgical repair or EVAR.

questions.question: A patient has an aortic dissection involving the ascending aorta. This is classified as:

options.explanation: Stanford type A dissection involves the ascending aorta, regardless of the site of origin. It requires urgent surgery.
Type B does not involve the ascending aorta.
DeBakey III is descending only.
That is a general term.
Intramural hematoma has no intimal tear.

explanation.overview: Stanford classification: Type A = any dissection involving the ascending aorta (proximal to the left subclavian). Type B = only descending aorta. Type A is a surgical emergency due to risk of tamponade, aortic regurgitation, and coronary occlusion.
explanation.highYield: Type A → surgery. Type B → medical (BP control) unless complicated (malperfusion, rupture).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: CT angiography determines the type and guides management.

questions.question: Which of the following is a common electrocardiographic finding in pericarditis?

options.text: Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression
options.explanation: Acute pericarditis typically shows concave‑upward ST elevation in multiple leads and PR depression.

options.text: ST elevation in a single coronary territory
options.explanation: Regional ST elevation suggests MI.
Q waves indicate infarction.
Peaked T waves suggest hyperkalemia.
Delta waves are seen in WPW syndrome.

explanation.overview: The ECG in acute pericarditis evolves through stages: stage 1 – diffuse ST elevation + PR depression; stage 2 – normalization; stage 3 – T‑wave inversion; stage 4 – normalization. Unlike MI, changes are diffuse and there are no reciprocal changes.
explanation.highYield: Pericarditis ECG: diffuse ST elevation, PR depression. Differentiate from MI (regional ST elevation).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Treatment with NSAIDs and colchicine typically resolves ECG changes.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about cardiac sarcoidosis?

options.text: It can present with conduction abnormalities, heart failure, and sudden death
options.explanation: Cardiac sarcoidosis involves non‑caseating granulomas that can infiltrate the conduction system and myocardium, causing heart block, ventricular arrhythmias, and cardiomyopathy.
It can be highly symptomatic.
It affects myocardium and conduction system.
Treatment is with corticosteroids and immunosuppression.
Sarcoidosis shows non‑caseating granulomas.

explanation.overview: Cardiac sarcoidosis is a granulomatous myocarditis that can manifest as heart block, ventricular tachycardia, heart failure, or sudden death. Diagnosis is by endomyocardial biopsy, cardiac MRI, or PET scan.
explanation.highYield: Sarcoidosis heart: non‑caseating granulomas, heart block, VT, restrictive CM. Treat with immunosuppression, ICD if needed.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Patients with known sarcoidosis should be screened for cardiac involvement.

questions.question: Which of the following is a potential complication of long‑standing aortic stenosis?

options.explanation: Heyde syndrome is the association between calcific aortic stenosis and angiodysplasia of the colon, leading to gastrointestinal bleeding due to acquired von Willebrand factor deficiency.
Cirrhosis is not directly caused by AS.
Renal failure is not a direct complication.
Pulmonary hypertension can develop secondary to left heart failure.
ASD is unrelated.

explanation.overview: Severe aortic stenosis can cause acquired von Willebrand factor deficiency due to shear stress‑induced proteolysis, leading to GI bleeding from angiodysplasia (Heyde syndrome). Valve replacement resolves the bleeding tendency.
explanation.highYield: Heyde syndrome: AS + angiodysplasia + bleeding. Acquired vWF deficiency. Resolves after valve replacement.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Workup of GI bleeding in elderly with AS should include evaluation for angiodysplasia and Heyde syndrome.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of acute mesenteric ischemia?

options.text: Sudden severe abdominal pain out of proportion to exam, with metabolic acidosis
options.explanation: Acute mesenteric ischemia, often due to superior mesenteric artery embolism, presents with severe pain, minimal early abdominal findings, and lactic acidosis.

options.text: Gradual onset of pain with diarrhea
options.explanation: That suggests inflammatory bowel disease.

options.text: Right lower quadrant pain with rebound
options.explanation: That suggests appendicitis.
That suggests pancreatitis.
That is biliary colic.

explanation.overview: Acute mesenteric ischemia is a vascular emergency. Embolism or thrombosis of the SMA leads to intestinal infarction. Pain is severe and out of proportion to the physical exam. Late findings include peritonitis and lactic acidosis.
explanation.highYield: Mesenteric ischemia: severe pain, diarrhea, bloody stools, lactic acidosis. Angiography or CT angio for diagnosis.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Urgent revascularization and resection of necrotic bowel.

questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of cardiac amyloidosis on cardiac MRI?

options.text: Diffuse late gadolinium enhancement and abnormal T1 mapping
options.explanation: Cardiac MRI in amyloidosis shows diffuse subendocardial or transmural LGE and elevated native T1 times, reflecting amyloid infiltration.
Subendocardial enhancement suggests ischemic injury.
Mid‑wall enhancement is seen in HCM or DCM, not typically amyloid.
T1 mapping is abnormal in amyloid.
Focal nodular is seen in sarcoidosis.

explanation.overview: Cardiac MRI is highly sensitive for cardiac amyloidosis. LGE pattern is typically diffuse, often with dark blood pool (difficulty nulling the myocardium). T1 mapping shows elevated extracellular volume.
explanation.highYield: Amyloid MRI: diffuse LGE, abnormal nulling, high native T1, expanded ECV. Helps differentiate from other causes of LVH.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: MRI is an important tool in the diagnostic algorithm for cardiac amyloidosis.

questions.question: Which of the following is a recognized complication of infective endocarditis?

options.explanation: Mycotic aneurysms result from septic emboli that lodge in vessel walls, causing infection and weakening of the arterial wall.
Atherosclerotic aneurysms are degenerative.
Berry aneurysms are congenital.
Dissection is unrelated to IE.
Syphilitic aneurysm is infectious but from syphilis.

explanation.overview: Mycotic aneurysms are infected aneurysms caused by septic emboli from infective endocarditis lodging in the vasa vasorum or vessel wall, leading to localized infection and dilation.
explanation.highYield: Mycotic aneurysm: complication of IE, often in cerebral or visceral arteries. Can rupture. Requires antibiotics and possibly surgery.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Any patient with IE and focal neurological symptoms or pain should be evaluated for mycotic aneurysm.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a typical cause of dilated cardiomyopathy?

options.explanation: Amyloidosis causes restrictive cardiomyopathy, not dilated.
Alcohol is a toxic cause.
Doxorubicin is a chemotherapeutic cause.
Myocarditis can lead to DCM.
Iron overload causes DCM.

explanation.overview: Dilated cardiomyopathy is characterized by ventricular dilation and systolic dysfunction. Causes include genetic, infectious, toxic, and metabolic. Amyloidosis and sarcoidosis typically cause restrictive cardiomyopathy.
explanation.highYield: DCM: dilated, poor EF. Restrictive: stiff, good EF but diastolic dysfunction. Amyloid → restrictive.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Echocardiography distinguishes DCM from restrictive CM.

questions.question: Which of the following is a typical feature of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy?

options.text: Apical ballooning in the absence of significant coronary artery disease
options.explanation: Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy is characterized by transient apical ballooning of the left ventricle, often after emotional stress, without obstructive CAD.
That is HCM.
That is ARVC.
That is hypertensive heart disease.
That is Kawasaki disease.

explanation.overview: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, also called broken heart syndrome, mimics acute MI but with normal coronaries. It presents with apical hypokinesis and hypercontractile base, often triggered by severe emotional or physical stress.
explanation.highYield: Takotsubo: postmenopausal women, chest pain, ST elevation, normal coronaries, apical ballooning. Reversible. Supportive care.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Most patients recover fully within weeks.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of rheumatic mitral regurgitation?

options.text: Leaflet thickening, chordal shortening, and annular dilation
options.explanation: Rheumatic MR results from leaflet fibrosis, retraction, and chordal shortening, preventing proper coaptation.
That is mitral valve prolapse.
That is infective endocarditis.
Commissural fusion causes stenosis.
Annular calcification alone is usually degenerative.

explanation.overview: Rheumatic heart disease can cause both mitral stenosis and regurgitation. In chronic MR, the valve leaflets are thickened, scarred, and retracted, with fused chordae, leading to a central regurgitant jet.
explanation.highYield: Rheumatic MR: thickened, retracted leaflets, chordal shortening. Often mixed with MS.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Rheumatic valve disease often requires surgical repair or replacement.

questions.question: Which of the following is a known side effect of amiodarone?

options.explanation: Amiodarone can cause pulmonary toxicity, including interstitial pneumonitis and pulmonary fibrosis, which can be fatal.
Amiodarone is used to treat arrhythmias, rarely causing TdP.
Amiodarone can cause hypotension but not hypertension.
Renal toxicity is not a major side effect.
Myopathy is less common.

explanation.overview: Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic with numerous side effects, including pulmonary fibrosis, thyroid dysfunction (hypo‑ or hyperthyroidism), liver toxicity, corneal deposits, and skin discoloration.
explanation.highYield: Amiodarone toxicity: pulmonary fibrosis (most feared), thyroid, liver, skin, cornea. Requires regular monitoring of PFTs, thyroid, LFTs.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Patients with unexplained dyspnea or cough on amiodarone need evaluation for pulmonary toxicity.
